items.source_locator: Chapter 5, §5.3 Stress & Coping > Coping Strategies (adaptive vs maladaptive coping; problem-focused coping; seeking social support).
items.source_version: Open RN Nursing Health Promotion, 2025 edition on NCBI Bookshelf; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Seeking accurate information, using social support, and developing practical self-management strategies are adaptive coping behaviors when they help the client engage with the illness and daily functioning. They are distinct from avoidance, denial, or other strategies that interfere with care or adjustment.

items.source_locator: §2.1 Important Dosage and Administration Instructions; §2.3 Initial Dosage; §5.2 Life-Threatening Respiratory Depression; §5.7 elderly/cachectic/debilitated patients; §8.5 Geriatric Use.
items.source_version: DailyMed SPL setid 300b6afd-bac8-32ca-e063-6294a90a12a7; page updated 2025-12-23; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Older adults can have increased opioid sensitivity and reduced renal, hepatic, or cardiac reserve. Morphine should be individualized, generally starting cautiously at the low end in geriatric patients, then titrated to analgesic effect while monitoring sedation, respiratory depression, renal function, concomitant sedatives, and other risk factors.

items.source_locator: Recommendations 1.4.12 and 1.5.11: excessive contraction frequency and conservative measures, including reducing or stopping oxytocin when used.
items.source_version: NICE NG229, published 2022-12-14 and last updated 2026-03-25; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Six contractions in 10 minutes averaged over 30 minutes meets the definition of uterine tachysystole. When tachysystole occurs during oxytocin administration—especially with recurrent fetal heart-rate decelerations—the oxytocin should be reduced or stopped according to protocol and intrauterine resuscitative measures and prompt reassessment initiated.

items.source_locator: Indications and Dosage: prevention of Rh immunization in unsensitized Rh-negative women; antepartum prophylaxis at 26–28 weeks and postpartum prophylaxis when indicated.
items.source_version: FDA RhoGAM labeling displayed by DailyMed, revised 07/2025; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Rho(D) immune globulin provides passive anti-D that suppresses maternal immunization after exposure to Rh-positive fetal red cells. It prevents sensitization; it does not treat established fetal hemolytic disease or change fetal Rh type. Antepartum prophylaxis does not automatically eliminate postpartum dosing when the newborn is Rh-positive.

items.source_name: CDC — Guidelines for Vaccinating Pregnant Women
items.source_locator: MMR section: live attenuated MMR is contraindicated during pregnancy; vaccinate after pregnancy when indicated.
items.source_version: CDC official pregnancy-vaccination guidance; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: MMR is a live attenuated viral vaccine and is contraindicated during pregnancy because of theoretical fetal risk. A rubella-nonimmune pregnant patient should receive MMR after pregnancy when indicated. Tdap and inactivated influenza vaccination are recommended during pregnancy according to current schedules.

items.source_locator: Warnings and Precautions — Hyperkalemia; potassium supplementation and potassium-containing salt substitutes increase risk; monitor serum potassium.
items.source_version: DailyMed FDA label setid 768563dc-a619-44dc-b97f-1a7e71fd56a0; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Spironolactone reduces potassium excretion and can cause hyperkalemia. Current labeling specifically identifies potassium supplementation and potassium-containing salt substitutes as risk enhancers and recommends serum-potassium monitoring after initiation/titration and regularly thereafter.

items.source_locator: Warnings/Monitoring serum theophylline concentrations and Drug Interactions — erythromycin decreases theophylline clearance and may increase serum concentrations.
items.source_version: DailyMed FDA label setid 699a4e05-95cb-4b28-8927-d97a4afbf463; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range. Nausea/vomiting, tremor, palpitations and tachyarrhythmias can occur with excessive exposure. Erythromycin can inhibit theophylline clearance and raise concentrations. When toxicity is suspected, labeling advises withholding additional theophylline and measuring the serum concentration promptly.

items.source_locator: BOXED WARNING — Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea/colitis; evaluate significant diarrhea during or after therapy.
items.source_version: DailyMed label version 35, updated 2026-04-08; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: New frequent watery diarrhea and cramping during clindamycin therapy require evaluation for C. difficile-associated diarrhea. The boxed warning notes that CDAD can be severe or fatal and can occur even after antibiotic exposure. Unsupervised antimotility treatment or simply continuing therapy without assessment can be unsafe.

items.source_locator: BOXED WARNING — prolonged tocolysis; maternal cardiovascular/metabolic adverse reactions including tachycardia/arrhythmias, pulmonary edema, hypokalemia and hyperglycemia.
items.source_version: Current FDA terbutaline injection label displayed by DailyMed; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Terbutaline is a beta-agonist and can cause maternal tachycardia, arrhythmias, pulmonary edema, myocardial ischemia, hypokalemia, and hyperglycemia. It is not FDA-approved for prolonged tocolysis beyond 48–72 hours and must not be used for outpatient maintenance tocolysis. New cardiovascular or respiratory symptoms require urgent review.

items.source_locator: BOXED WARNING / Warnings and Precautions — tendinitis and tendon rupture; discontinue immediately for serious fluoroquinolone adverse reactions/tendon symptoms.
items.source_version: DailyMed CIPRO label setid 888dc7f9-ad9c-4c00-8d50-8ddfd9bd27c0, version 32; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Fluoroquinolones, including ciprofloxacin, can cause tendinitis and tendon rupture, sometimes with disabling or irreversible adverse effects. New tendon pain or swelling during therapy warrants stopping the fluoroquinolone and prompt clinical review, with avoidance of exercise or loading of the affected tendon until evaluated.

items.source_locator: BOXED WARNING — Tardive Dyskinesia: risk rises with duration/cumulative dose; discontinue if signs develop; avoid treatment longer than 12 weeks except rare cases.
items.source_version: DailyMed FDA metoclopramide label updated in 2026; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Repetitive involuntary lip and tongue movements after prolonged metoclopramide exposure are concerning for tardive dyskinesia. The 2026 boxed warning states that TD can be potentially irreversible, risk increases with treatment duration and cumulative dose, and metoclopramide should be discontinued if signs or symptoms develop.

items.source_locator: Prevention Strategies > Hand Hygiene and Aseptic Technique; Skin Preparation; Catheter Site Dressing Regimens.
items.source_version: CDC official intravascular-catheter infection-prevention guidance; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: CDC recommends hand hygiene and aseptic technique when dressing an intravascular catheter. For dressing changes, either clean or sterile gloves are acceptable; maximal sterile barrier precautions are required for central-line insertion, not every routine dressing change. The site is disinfected with the recommended antiseptic and covered with a sterile dressing.
items.ncsbn_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hand hygiene, aseptic technique, and infection-control precautions.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_locator: II. Proper Techniques for Urinary Catheter Insertion: aseptic technique and sterile equipment in acute care.
items.source_version: CDC CAUTI Summary of Recommendations; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: In acute-care hospitals, CDC recommends aseptic urinary-catheter insertion using sterile equipment. The recommended setup includes sterile gloves, drape and sponges, an appropriate antiseptic or sterile solution for periurethral cleaning, and a single-use lubricant packet.
items.ncsbn_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — aseptic technique and use of infection-control precautions.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_name: The Joint Commission — Emergency Cart / Defibrillator Readiness
items.source_locator: Standards FAQ — crash-cart defibrillators/high-risk equipment and organizational processes for monitoring emergency-cart readiness.
items.source_version: Joint Commission Standards FAQ updated 2026-04-21; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Emergency carts must be kept ready for immediate use under a defined organizational monitoring process. An expired medication and inadequately charged defibrillator undermine readiness and require correction or use of the facility's backup process. A national rule does not require the same 'start of every shift' frequency in every organization.
items.ncsbn_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — verify safe use/function of equipment and maintain client safety.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_locator: Portable Extinguishers > Use: identify a safe evacuation path, select correct extinguisher, PASS method, evacuate when fire is beyond incipient stage or control is doubtful.
items.source_version: OSHA official eTool guidance; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: OSHA recommends confirming a safe evacuation path before approaching a fire, selecting the appropriate extinguisher, and using PASS: pull the pin, aim low at the base, squeeze the handle, and sweep side to side. If the extinguisher is empty, the fire grows, or the user is unsure of safe control, evacuation is the priority.

items.source_locator: Environmental infection-control measures — frequently touched surfaces near patients and patient-care equipment require priority/frequent cleaning and disinfection.
items.source_version: CDC Isolation Precautions guidance maintained on current site; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Frequently touched surfaces close to the patient accumulate repeated hand contact and are more likely to participate in contact transmission. CDC specifically highlights bedrails, bedside tables, commodes, doorknobs, sinks, and nearby equipment for appropriate routine cleaning and disinfection.
items.ncsbn_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — infection-control precautions and environmental safety.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_name: CDC — Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices
items.source_locator: Standard Precautions — PPE selection/use and hand hygiene; remove PPE to avoid self-contamination and perform hand hygiene after removal.
items.source_version: CDC Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: The safety goal during doffing is to prevent self-contamination. CDC provides example sequences, but the exact order can vary with the PPE ensemble and isolation workflow. Staff should use the approved sequence, avoid touching contaminated PPE surfaces to skin or clothing, dispose of PPE appropriately, and perform hand hygiene.
items.ncsbn_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — PPE and hand hygiene.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_name: OSHA — 29 CFR 1904.8 Needlestick and Sharps Injuries
items.source_locator: 29 CFR 1904.8(a) and 1904.8(b): record work-related contaminated needlestick/sharps injuries and protect worker privacy; applies to employers subject to Part 1904 recordkeeping.
items.source_version: OSHA 29 CFR 1904.8 current regulation page; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: OSHA requires work-related needlestick injuries from sharps contaminated with another person's blood or other potentially infectious material to be recorded when the employer is subject to Part 1904 recordkeeping. Such employers also maintain sharps-injury information while protecting employee confidentiality. Not every medical office is subject to the sharps-log requirement.

items.source_name: CDC — Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices
items.source_locator: Standard Precautions and 5a Hand Hygiene: apply to all patient care/settings; PPE is based on anticipated exposure.
items.source_version: CDC Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Standard Precautions are the baseline infection-prevention practices for every patient regardless of known infection status. They include hand hygiene and a task-specific risk assessment for gloves, gown, mask and eye/face protection based on anticipated exposure to blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, nonintact skin, or contaminated material.
items.ncsbn_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — Standard Precautions and hand hygiene.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_locator: About the POLST Form — portable medical orders for people with progressing serious illness/advanced frailty; state programs/forms and legal requirements vary.
items.source_version: National POLST guidance current through 2025-12; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: POLST is intended for people with progressing serious illness or advanced frailty and converts current treatment preferences into medical orders for emergencies and transitions. An advance directive serves broader advance-planning purposes. State laws, terminology, forms, and portability requirements differ, so a generic form is not automatically valid everywhere.
items.ncsbn_locator: Management of Care — Advance Directives / client rights and care preferences.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_name: CDC — Clinical Safety: Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers
items.source_locator: Recommendations > Know when to clean your hands: after touching a patient or the patient’s surroundings.
items.source_version: CDC Clinical Safety hand-hygiene page dated 2024-02-27; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: The WHO Five Moments include hand hygiene after touching the patient's surroundings. Adjusting equipment such as an IV pump within the patient zone can create a hand-hygiene indication even if the patient was not directly touched.
items.ncsbn_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hand hygiene; classification cross-check.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_locator: Impact Wellbeing Guide — systems-level approach to healthcare-worker wellbeing; address staffing, schedules, administrative burden, leadership and operational drivers rather than relying only on individual resilience.
items.source_version: NIOSH Impact Wellbeing Guide revised 07/2024; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: NIOSH's Impact Wellbeing approach explicitly moves beyond placing the burden on individual resilience. Hospital leaders should examine and improve workplace operations, including staffing and workload, schedule control, administrative burden, safety, communication, and access to support. Individual self-care can complement but not replace system-level improvement.

items.source_name: NCSBN — National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation
items.source_locator: National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation — responsibilities of delegating nurse/employer/delegatee; licensed nurse retains supervision/evaluation responsibility; jurisdictional laws/rules govern delegation.
items.source_version: NCSBN delegation guidance current on official site; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Delegating measurement of routine vital signs does not transfer the RN's responsibility for nursing assessment, clinical judgment, supervision, and follow-up. A newly abnormal result requires the RN to evaluate the change and decide what additional assessment or escalation is needed, within the jurisdiction's delegation rules and facility policy.
items.ncsbn_locator: Management of Care — Assignment, Delegation and Supervision; rights of delegation and evaluation.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_locator: Disclosure of Errors primer — transparent disclosure, including nonharmful errors, with institutional support and structured disclosure processes.
items.source_version: AHRQ PSNet primer reviewed/current through 2024; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: An error that reaches a patient should trigger immediate clinical assessment and the organization's safety-response process even when no injury is apparent. Patient-safety guidance supports transparent disclosure rather than concealment. The nurse should promptly notify appropriate clinical/safety leaders and participate in disclosure according to organizational policy rather than independently speculating about causation.
items.ncsbn_locator: Management of Care and Safety — acknowledge/document errors and report client safety issues.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_locator: Management of Care > Assignment, Delegation and Supervision: prioritize client acuity; assign/delegate based on client needs, staff competency and scope; evaluate delegated care.
items.source_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Safe assignments depend on more than the number of patients. ANA staffing principles emphasize patient acuity and care intensity, nurse competence and skill mix, workload, available support and resources, and changing unit conditions. A complex wound-care client and an unstable client may create very different workload demands from stable patients.
items.ncsbn_locator: Management of Care — Assignment, Delegation and Supervision; prioritize acuity and assign by client needs/competency.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_locator: Professional Boundaries and Social Media guidance — maintain professional boundaries online; client initiation does not make a personal relationship appropriate; do not accept client friend requests on personal social media.
items.source_version: NCSBN professional-boundaries guidance current on official site; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: NCSBN advises maintaining professional boundaries in electronic media and using caution with online social contact with patients and former patients. A patient initiating contact does not automatically make a personal relationship appropriate. The safest response is to preserve the professional boundary and follow employer and board-of-nursing guidance.
items.ncsbn_locator: Management of Care — ethical practice and professional boundaries.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_name: HHS ODPHP — Healthy People 2030: Social Determinants of Health
items.source_locator: Social Determinants of Health — conditions in environments affecting health; examples include safe housing and transportation and their effect on healthcare access/outcomes.
items.source_version: Healthy People 2030 official HHS/ODPHP page; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Healthy People 2030 identifies housing and transportation as social determinants of health and notes that transportation barriers can interfere with access to care and worsen outcomes. Therefore, option B best explains why the barriers belong in discharge planning even when the client understands the instructions. Option A incorrectly waits for a direct complication and minimizes transportation as merely scheduling. Option C misclassifies access barriers as health-literacy problems despite the client understanding the plan. Option D confuses social determinants with utilization management and payer authorization.

items.source_name: ACOG — Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy
items.source_locator: Preeclampsia FAQ — hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or other organ-injury features; severe headache/visual changes are severe-feature warning symptoms.
items.source_version: ACOG official patient guidance current on site; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: ACOG describes preeclampsia as hypertension arising after 20 weeks with findings such as proteinuria and identifies severe headache and visual changes as severe features. Option A is therefore the best classification even though the blood pressure itself is below the severe-range threshold. Option B incorrectly ignores severe neurologic features. Option C is inferior because proteinuria supports preeclampsia rather than isolated gestational hypertension. Option D is incorrect because chronic hypertension is present before pregnancy or develops before 20 weeks, not first recognized at 32 weeks in a previously normotensive client.

items.source_name: Merck Manual Professional — Vaginal Bleeding During Late Pregnancy
items.source_locator: Etiology table/differential — placenta previa classically causes painless bright-red bleeding; placental abruption more often causes pain/tenderness.
items.source_version: Merck Manual Professional current page; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Merck describes placenta previa as sudden painless bright-red bleeding with minimal or no uterine tenderness. Option D best fits the full pattern. Option A is less consistent because placental abruption more often produces abdominal pain or uterine tenderness, although visible bleeding may underestimate severity. Option B is less likely because vasa previa classically presents with painless bleeding plus fetal instability, often around membrane rupture; this client has intact membranes and a reassuring tracing. Option C is less consistent because bloody show is typically a small amount of blood-tinged mucus associated with cervical change rather than sudden unexplained bright-red bleeding.

items.source_locator: Terms used in this guideline > Precipitate labour: baby born less than 3 hours after the start of uterine contractions.
items.source_version: NICE NG207 published 2021; official current guideline accessed/rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: NCBI Bookshelf's current Open RN labor-and-delivery chapter defines precipitous labor as labor and delivery that are extremely rapid, usually less than 3 hours from the start of contractions to birth, so option A fits. Option B cannot be established from total labor duration because tachysystole is defined by contraction frequency over time. Option C is the opposite pattern: an arrest disorder requires absent cervical progress, not rapid dilation followed by birth. Option D is incorrect because multiparity may shorten labor but does not remove a sub-3-hour course from the precipitous-labor definition.

items.source_locator: The Apgar Score — five components are color, heart rate, reflexes, muscle tone, and respiration; reported at 1 and 5 minutes.
items.source_version: Joint ACOG/AAP Committee Opinion on Apgar scoring; currentness rechecked on official sources 2026-08-15.
items.finding: The joint ACOG/AAP statement defines the five Apgar components as color, heart rate, reflexes or reflex irritability, muscle tone, and respiration or respiratory effort, making option D correct. Option A substitutes blood pressure, temperature, and birth weight. Option B substitutes gestational age, birth weight, and head circumference. Option C substitutes oxygen saturation, blood glucose, and temperature. Those measurements may be clinically relevant to newborn assessment but are not components of the Apgar score.

items.source_locator: Symptoms — fever, headache, stiff neck and photophobia; bacterial meningitis can worsen rapidly and requires immediate evaluation.
items.source_version: CDC About Meningitis updated 2025-09-09; currentness cross-checked against CDC meningococcal clinical guidance dated 2026-06-04 and rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: CDC identifies fever, headache, and stiff neck as common features of meningococcal meningitis, and photophobia can accompany meningitis; prompt diagnosis and treatment are important. Option A therefore best matches the complete infectious meningeal cluster. Option B can cause abrupt severe headache and meningeal irritation but does not as well explain the fever in this presentation. Option C can cause headache and photophobia but does not account well for fever with true nuchal rigidity. Option D may cause fever and generalized aches but does not adequately explain this combination of severe headache, photophobia, and nuchal rigidity.

items.source_name: European Association of Urology — Paediatric Urology: Acute Scrotum
items.source_locator: Acute Scrotum / Testicular torsion — sudden severe pain with nausea/vomiting; critical ischemic window; Doppler should not delay urgent surgical treatment when torsion is suspected.
items.source_version: Current EAU Paediatric Urology guideline accessed/rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: The EAU guideline identifies testicular torsion as a paediatric urologic emergency requiring immediate treatment and states that outcome is best when intervention occurs as early as possible, ideally within 4–6 hours. Option B is therefore the best action. Option A is inferior because Doppler ultrasonography is useful but should not delay intervention when torsion is strongly suspected. Option C risks a dangerous delay by treating presumed epididymitis without first resolving the torsion emergency. Option D is unsafe because manual detorsion may be attempted while awaiting surgery, but symptom improvement does not replace urgent surgical exploration and fixation.

items.source_locator: Urinary Retention — acute retention may cause painful distention; prostate/outlet obstruction is a common male cause; acute retention is relieved by urethral catheterization unless contraindicated.
items.source_version: MSD Manual Professional full review 2026-03; updated 2026-04; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Current MSD Manual guidance describes acute urinary retention as cessation of urination that can cause abdominal distention and pain; prostate abnormalities are a common cause of outlet obstruction in men, and relief of acute retention requires urethral catheterization. Option C therefore best fits the presentation and management. Option A does not explain the full painful distended-bladder retention syndrome and would delay decompression. Option B describes upper-tract obstruction and does not best account for a palpable distended bladder with complete inability to void. Option D misclassifies an acute painful inability to void as chronic retention and delays required decompression.

items.source_name: American College of Radiology — ACR Manual on Contrast Media 2026
items.source_locator: Treatment of Contrast Reactions / Adult Acute Reaction Tables — severe allergic-like reactions require immediate emergency treatment; epinephrine is used for severe manifestations; corticosteroids are not useful for acute treatment.
items.source_version: ACR Manual on Contrast Media 2026; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: The ACR Manual on Contrast Media 2026 states that allergic-like iodinated contrast reactions can resemble true allergic reactions even when an antigen-antibody mechanism is not identified, that prior sensitization is not required, and that treatment of an allergic-like contrast reaction is identical to that of an equivalent allergic reaction. Option D is therefore correct; the adult treatment tables include epinephrine for severe manifestations. Option A inappropriately delays epinephrine and relies on corticosteroids, which ACR states are not useful for acute treatment. Option B incorrectly reclassifies an allergic-like presentation as physiologic. Option C risks delaying indicated emergency therapy.

items.source_name: ACOG — Intrapartum Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring
items.source_locator: Fetal heart tracing definitions — normal baseline fetal heart rate 110–160 beats/min.
items.source_version: ACOG definitions currentness rechecked against Clinical Practice Guideline No. 10, October 2025; rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: ACOG's fetal heart tracing definitions identify a normal baseline fetal heart rate as 110–160 beats/min and use the three-tier Category I/II/III framework. Option D is therefore correct. Option A includes values below the bradycardia threshold. Option B widens both the lower and upper limits beyond the standard range. Option C excludes normal values from 110–119 and includes values above the tachycardia threshold. Currentness was rechecked against ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 10 from October 2025, which continues to use the three-tier intrapartum classification framework.

items.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Hospital Stay for Healthy Term Newborn Infants
items.source_locator: Recommendations, minimum discharge criteria item 2 — awake heart rate 100–190 beats/min; sleeping quietly can be as low as 70 without compromise.
items.source_version: AAP Pediatrics policy statement; official source currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: For a healthy term newborn, the AAP lists an awake heart rate of 100–190 beats/min; sleeping quietly can produce lower rates. Because this stem now specifies an awake newborn, 140 beats/min is within the expected range, while 90 beats/min is below the cited awake range. The state qualifier removes the prior second-answer ambiguity created by lower acceptable sleeping heart rates.

items.source_name: American Heart Association — Treating Arrhythmias in Children
items.source_locator: Normal ranges for children — infants average 100–190 beats/min at rest; older children/teenagers typically 60–100 beats/min.
items.source_version: AHA page last reviewed 2024-10-29; currentness rechecked against 2025 AHA pediatric resuscitation resources on 2026-08-15.
items.finding: The American Heart Association notes that normal resting heart rate differs by pediatric age: infants average substantially faster rates than older children and teenagers. Option B correctly applies age-dependent interpretation. Option A incorrectly treats pediatric ages as sharing one range. Option C reverses the normal age trend. Option D incorrectly assumes adult limits apply soon after infancy.

items.source_name: American Society of Hematology — VTE Diagnosis Guideline
items.source_locator: Testing for Blood Clots / DVT diagnosis pathway — a positive D-dimer alone does not diagnose DVT; appropriate imaging such as ultrasound is required according to pretest probability.
items.source_version: ASH VTE diagnosis guideline patient-version 2023; parent guideline remains under expert monitoring; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: ASH guidance states that a positive D-dimer means a clot may be present but should not be used to diagnose DVT by itself; further testing is required, and ultrasound is recommended in the appropriate lower-extremity DVT pathway. Option D is correct. Option A incorrectly treats a positive result as confirmatory. Option B reverses the interpretation of a positive result. Option C incorrectly removes D-dimer from validated VTE diagnostic strategies.

items.source_locator: ESR results — faster ESR can indicate more inflammation, but ESR alone cannot diagnose the condition causing inflammation.
items.source_version: MedlinePlus ESR page updated 2024-12-02; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: MedlinePlus explains that ESR can show that inflammation is present but cannot diagnose which condition is causing it. Option A is therefore correct. Option B overstates specificity and incorrectly identifies bacterial infection as the cause without corroboration. Option C misinterprets an elevated ESR as improved immune function. Option D reverses the relationship because faster sedimentation can accompany higher levels of inflammation.

items.source_locator: Apgar Score table — color: all blue/pale=0, pink body with blue extremities=1, all pink=2.
items.source_version: Merck Manual Professional Apgar table current on 2026 site; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: Merck's June 2026 Apgar table assigns 1 point for color when the body is pink and the extremities are blue. Option B matches the scoring criterion. Option A would correspond to an infant who is blue or pale overall. Option C requires the infant to be all pink for 2 points. Option D is incorrect because color remains one of the five Apgar components; oxygen saturation is not substituted for it in the standard score.

items.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — HealthyChildren.org: Umbilical Cord Care
items.source_locator: Umbilical Cord Care — keep stump clean and dry, fold diaper below it for air exposure, use sponge baths until stump separates.
items.source_version: AAP HealthyChildren official guidance; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: AAP guidance recommends dry cord care: keep the stump clean and dry, fold the diaper below it to promote air exposure, and use sponge baths until the cord separates. Option B therefore best reflects routine home care. Option A adds routine alcohol and gauze that are not recommended for an uncomplicated stump. Option C keeps the stump moist and covered, contrary to dry-cord care. Option D introduces tub bathing while the stump remains attached rather than using sponge baths.
items.ncsbn_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — Ante-/Intra-/Postpartum and Newborn Care; assist with learning newborn care.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_locator: Perineal pain after vaginal delivery — cold/ice packs for 10–20 minutes are most effective in the first 24–72 hours for swelling and pain.
items.source_version: ACOG Postpartum Pain Management guidance current on official site; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: ACOG supports cold/ice packs for short intervals to reduce perineal swelling and pain after vaginal birth, with greatest usefulness during the first 24–72 hours. At 8 hours postpartum, an ice pack is therefore appropriate. The alternatives either withhold useful care or incorrectly prefer immediate/continuous heat for acute swelling.

items.source_name: ACOG — Can I sleep on my back when I’m pregnant?
items.source_locator: Ask ACOG — in the second and third trimesters, supine positioning can compress a major vessel and cause dizziness/reduce blood flow; side positioning is recommended.
items.source_version: ACOG pregnancy guidance currentness rechecked against material reviewed 2026-02 and accessed 2026-08-15.
items.finding: ACOG explains that lying flat in later pregnancy can allow the gravid uterus to compress a major vessel, reducing venous return and causing dizziness; turning to either side relieves the positional compression. Option B directly addresses the likely mechanism. Option A maintains the provoking position. Option C assumes hypoglycemia without evidence and does not first correct the positional cause. Option D delays the needed repositioning while the client remains symptomatic.

items.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Nursing Assistant: Provide for Personal Care Needs of Clients
items.source_locator: Bathing procedure — begin with face/neck and cleaner body areas, progress through body/legs, and perform perineal care last to reduce transfer of pathogens.
items.source_version: NCBI Bookshelf nursing-assistant educational procedure; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: The NCBI Bookshelf nursing-assistant procedure describes a head-to-toe bath sequence that begins with the face and neck and leaves perineal care until the end to reduce pathogen transfer from a more contaminated area. Option A follows that sequence. Option B starts with the perineum and increases cross-contamination risk. Option C places perineal care before cleaner regions are finished. Option D disregards the clean-to-dirty sequence.
items.ncsbn_locator: Basic Care and Comfort — assist with hygiene/activities of daily living; exact bath sequence requires procedure source.
items.ncsbn_version: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan, effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.source_name: ACOG — Patient Screening for Perinatal Mental Health
items.source_locator: Clinical Practice Guideline No. 4 implementation — use standardized validated screening for depression/anxiety at prenatal and postpartum contacts with systems for assessment, treatment and follow-up.
items.source_version: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 4 issued 2023-06; implementation page currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: ACOG recommends screening patients receiving postpartum care for depression and anxiety with standardized, validated instruments and having systems in place for timely assessment, treatment, and follow-up. Option D matches that guidance even when the client does not volunteer symptoms. Option A incorrectly limits screening to symptomatic clients. Option B omits recommended postpartum screening. Option C incorrectly removes screening from routine obstetric care.

items.source_locator: Signs of a good latch — wide-open mouth over the areola, lips turned outward, chin touching the breast, with effective swallowing.
items.source_version: CDC newborn breastfeeding guidance currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: CDC breastfeeding guidance describes a good latch as a wide-open mouth taking in the areola, lips turned outward, and the chin against the breast. Option A matches those findings. Option B describes inward lips and poor positioning. Option C describes a shallow nipple-only latch and clicking, which suggest ineffective attachment. Option D describes persistent pain and inward cheek movement, findings that warrant latch reassessment.

items.source_name: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force — Cervical Cancer: Screening
items.source_locator: Current final cervical-cancer screening recommendation — screening depends on age, test strategy, prior history and risk; update is in progress and draft/future intervals are not treated as final.
items.source_version: USPSTF 2018 final recommendation remains current while update is in progress as of 2026-08-15; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: The current USPSTF cervical-cancer screening recommendation uses age and screening-test strategy to determine routine intervals and identifies higher-risk situations that require individualized follow-up; prior screening history also affects decisions such as when screening can stop. Option C best reflects that framework. Option A incorrectly applies annual screening to everyone. Option B stops after one normal result without regard to recommended intervals or history. Option D ignores guideline-based age, test, and risk criteria.

items.source_locator: Baby blues — commonly begin about 2–3 days after birth and usually improve within a few days to 1–2 weeks; persistent/severe symptoms require evaluation.
items.source_version: ACOG Postpartum Depression FAQ reviewed 2025-12; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: ACOG notes that postpartum baby blues commonly begin a few days after delivery and usually improve within days to one or two weeks without treatment. Option B fits the timing, mild symptoms, and spontaneous resolution. Option A and D describe depression despite a short, self-limited course. Option C is inconsistent with the absence of severe psychotic symptoms and the benign resolution.

items.source_locator: Bereavement care — individualize support; offer parents the opportunity to hold the baby and participate in cultural or religious rituals according to their preferences.
items.source_version: ACOG/SMFM Obstetric Care Consensus Management of Stillbirth, reaffirmed 2025; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.finding: ACOG/SMFM stillbirth guidance recommends individualized bereavement care and giving parents the opportunity to hold the baby and participate in desired cultural or religious activities. Option D follows that approach without making contact obligatory. Option A restricts contact rather than offering choice. Option B ignores individual, cultural, and religious needs. Option C postpones supportive options that should be discussed during the hospitalization.
